notes: Every lower-body session begins with 8–10 minutes of stationary bike warm-up at easy resistance before working sets.
Warm-up includes ankle circles, hip circles, and supine knee slides before working sets on lower-body days.
Week 3 onwards: Terminal Knee Extension with band added at the START of each lower-body session as a VMO activation drill.
Phase 2 warm-up: TKE band work and bodyweight glute bridges performed before loading on lower-body days.
Phase 3 warm-up: TKE band work, glute bridges, and Wall Sit (30 seconds at 60°) added as ski-specific isometric primer before working sets.
Three training days per week in Phase 1 (Weeks 1–4) with at least one rest day between sessions.
Four training days per week in Phases 2 and 3 (Weeks 5–12), split into two lower-body and two upper-body days.
Week 4 is a deload week: reduce all working sets by one and drop loads by ~15%.
Week 8 is a deload week: same protocol as Week 4.
Week 12 is a deload and full movement reassessment week.
Week 11 is the peak loading week — push all compound lifts to heaviest loads with excellent form.
If knee pain or swelling exceeds 3/10 post-session, regress previous session's loading by 10–15% before progressing.
If swelling is present before a session, do not progress load — maintain or regress.
On rest days, 20–30 minutes of low-intensity activity (walking, easy cycling, or swimming) is prescribed rather than complete inactivity.
Post-session: 10–15 minutes of ice if knee is warm or mildly swollen; elevation for 20 minutes post-session in early phases.
Post-session mobility: 5–10 minutes of hip flexor stretching, calf/Achilles stretching, and thoracic spine rotation after every session.
Daily monitoring: client rates knee pain and swelling on 0–10 scale before and after every session.
Protein intake should be distributed across 3–4 meals per day rather than concentrated in one sitting.
Collagen peptides (15 g) with vitamin C (50 mg) taken 30–60 minutes before training.
Client should eat at or slightly above maintenance calories — not in a caloric deficit during this programme.
Skater Squat (Week 10) should only be introduced if client is completely pain-free on all Phase 3 exercises.
Bulgarian Split Squat (Week 7): if any discomfort, revert to goblet squat and revisit in Week 9.
Barbell Back Squat (Week 9): if client is uncomfortable with bar position, use safety squat bar or continue goblet squat at increased load.
Single-leg balance test (right leg, eyes closed, 30 seconds) to be assessed informally at the end of each phase.
Return-to-skiing requires surgeon and physiotherapist sign-off regardless of physical benchmark achievement.

# 12-Week Strength & Ski-Return Programme
### Client Profile: 36M | Recreational Lifter | Post-Medial Meniscus Repair (6 months)
### Clearance: Low-impact strength work | No jumping | No deep knee flexion under load

---

## PROGRAMME OVERVIEW

The programme is divided into three four-week phases, each building logically on the last. The overarching philosophy is **joint-first loading**: every exercise selection earns its place by either protecting the healing meniscus, building the muscular armour around the knee, or developing the whole-body strength and stability that skiing demands. Depth, load, and complexity increase only when the previous phase has been mastered without pain or swelling.

**Key constraints honoured throughout:**
- Knee flexion under load kept to approximately 0–60° in Phase 1, progressing to ~70–80° in Phase 2, and ~80–90° in Phase 3 — never a full squat depth
- No plyometrics, box jumps, or impact loading
- Bilateral before unilateral; machines before free-weight equivalents where appropriate early on
- Daily monitoring: ask the client to rate knee pain and swelling on a 0–10 scale before and after every session. If either exceeds 3/10 post-session, regress the previous session's loading by 10–15% before progressing again

---

## PHASE 1 — WEEKS 1–4
### *Foundation: Tissue Tolerance, Motor Control, and Baseline Strength*

The goal of this phase is to re-educate the muscles that protect the knee — the VMO, glutes, and hamstrings — while building general upper-body and posterior-chain strength. Loads are deliberately conservative. The client should finish every session feeling worked but not wrecked. Three training days per week with at least one rest day between sessions.

**Session structure each week:** Day A | Rest | Day B | Rest | Day C | Rest | Rest

---

### WEEK 1

**Day A — Lower Body Focus**

Begin every lower-body session with 8–10 minutes of low-impact warm-up: stationary bike at easy resistance, keeping the seat high enough that the knee never flexes beyond 60°. Follow with 5 minutes of gentle ankle circles, hip circles, and supine knee slides (heel slides on a smooth surface, sliding only to comfortable range).

*Working sets:*

- **Leg Press (feet high and wide, 0–50° range only)** — 3 sets × 12 reps at a load that feels like a 6/10 effort. The high foot placement shifts demand toward the glutes and hamstrings and away from the anterior knee. Instruct the client to stop the descent the moment he feels any anterior knee discomfort.
- **Seated Leg Curl** — 3 × 15. Hamstring strength is critical for meniscal offloading. Keep the movement smooth and controlled; avoid slamming the weight stack.
- **Hip Abduction Machine** — 3 × 15. Glute medius weakness is almost universal after a lower-limb injury and contributes to valgus collapse on the slopes.
- **Standing Hip Extension (cable, low pulley, ankle cuff)** — 3 × 12 each side. Glute max activation without knee stress.
- **Calf Raise (seated machine)** — 3 × 15. Gastrocnemius and soleus strength supports the knee joint passively.
- **Dead Bug** — 3 × 8 each side. Core stability foundation.

**Day B — Upper Body and Core**

- **Seated Cable Row** — 4 × 10
- **Dumbbell Bench Press** — 3 × 10
- **Lat Pulldown (neutral grip)** — 3 × 12
- **Dumbbell Shoulder Press** — 3 × 10
- **Cable Face Pull** — 3 × 15
- **Pallof Press** — 3 × 10 each side
- **Plank** — 3 × 30 seconds

**Day C — Full Body, Lower Emphasis**

- **Leg Press (same parameters as Day A)** — 3 × 10, slightly heavier than Day A if pain-free
- **Romanian Deadlift (RDL)** — 3 × 10. This is the cornerstone posterior-chain exercise for this programme. Hinge at the hip, soft knee, bar travels close to the legs. No knee flexion stress whatsoever. Start with a moderate dumbbell load to groove the pattern.
- **Seated Leg Curl** — 3 × 12
- **Single-Leg Hip Thrust (bodyweight, right leg supported on bench)** — 3 × 10 each side. Keep the right knee at roughly 90° but unloaded — the hip is doing the work. If 90° causes discomfort, reduce the bench height or use a step.
- **Seated Calf Raise** — 3 × 15
- **Cable Woodchop (low to high)** — 3 × 10 each side
- **Side Plank** — 3 × 20 seconds each side

---

### WEEKS 2–4 — PHASE 1 PROGRESSION

The exercise menu stays the same across Weeks 1–4. Progression is achieved through the following mechanisms:

**Week 2:** Add one working set to each main lower-body exercise (so 3 sets becomes 4). Increase upper-body loads by 2.5–5 kg where the final set felt easy. On the RDL, transition from dumbbells to a barbell if the pattern is clean.

**Week 3:** Introduce a tempo prescription on the leg press and leg curl — 3 seconds down, 1-second pause, 1 second up (written as 3-1-1). This increases time under tension without adding load stress to the joint. Reduce reps to 10 on the leg press to accommodate the tempo. Add a **Terminal Knee Extension (TKE) with band** — 3 × 15 each side — at the start of each lower-body session as a VMO activation drill. Loop a resistance band around a rack at knee height, step into it so it sits behind the knee, and perform small, controlled knee extensions from about 30° to full extension.

**Week 4:** Deload week. Reduce all working sets by one and drop loads by approximately 15%. The purpose is tissue recovery and consolidation. The client should feel fresh by the end of this week. Use the extra recovery capacity to focus on movement quality — video the RDL and leg press from the side and give technique feedback.

---

## PHASE 2 — WEEKS 5–8
### *Strength Development: Progressive Loading and Unilateral Introduction*

The client should now have a well-established movement vocabulary, a pain-free knee at the Phase 1 ranges, and a meaningful baseline of posterior-chain strength. Phase 2 introduces unilateral lower-body work, increases knee flexion range cautiously to approximately 70–80°, and shifts the rep ranges toward classic strength territory. Training frequency increases to four days per week, split into two lower-body days and two upper-body days.

**Session structure:** Day A (Lower) | Day B (Upper) | Rest | Day C (Lower) | Day D (Upper) | Rest | Rest

---

### WEEK 5

**Day A — Lower Body Strength**

Warm-up: 8 minutes stationary bike, seat height adjusted to allow up to 70° knee flexion. Add 5 minutes of TKE band work and bodyweight glute bridges before loading.

- **Leg Press (0–70° range, moderate load)** — 4 × 8. The increased range is the progression here; do not also increase load significantly in the same week.
- **Barbell RDL** — 4 × 8. This should now feel like a genuine strength exercise. Load progressively — aim for something that makes the last two reps of the final set genuinely challenging.
- **Seated Leg Curl** — 4 × 10
- **Step-Up (low box, 15–20 cm)** — 3 × 10 each side. This is the first unilateral knee-loading exercise. Use a low box so the knee flexion at the bottom of the step is minimal. Hold dumbbells for load. Drive through the heel of the elevated foot; do not push off the trailing leg.
- **Hip Thrust (barbell, bilateral)** — 4 × 10. Progress from the single-leg bodyweight version. The bilateral version allows heavier loading of the glutes with the knee at a fixed, comfortable angle.
- **Copenhagen Plank (modified — knees bent, lower knee on bench)** — 3 × 20 seconds each side. Adductor strength is often neglected and is important for medial knee stability.

**Day B — Upper Body Strength**

- **Barbell Bench Press** — 4 × 6
- **Weighted Pull-Up or Lat Pulldown** — 4 × 6–8
- **Seated Cable Row (close grip)** — 4 × 8
- **Dumbbell Incline Press** — 3 × 10
- **Cable Face Pull** — 3 × 15
- **Overhead Tricep Extension** — 3 × 12
- **Barbell Curl** — 3 × 12

**Day C — Lower Body Strength (Variation)**

- **Goblet Squat (to 70° depth, heels elevated 1–2 cm on plates)** — 4 × 8. The heel elevation reduces ankle dorsiflexion demand and keeps the torso more upright, reducing shear at the knee. The goblet position limits load naturally. This is the first true squat pattern in the programme. Monitor carefully.
- **Single-Leg RDL (dumbbell, right hand holds weight, left leg hinges)** — 3 × 10 each side. Introduces balance and hip stability demands.
- **Leg Press (single leg, right leg)** — 3 × 10. Allows you to identify and address any strength asymmetry between legs.
- **Seated Leg Curl** — 3 × 12
- **Lateral Band Walk** — 3 × 15 steps each direction. Glute medius endurance for ski-specific hip stability.
- **Pallof Press (standing)** — 3 × 10 each side

**Day D — Upper Body and Core**

- **Overhead Press (barbell)** — 4 × 6
- **Weighted Chin-Up** — 4 × 6
- **Dumbbell Row** — 4 × 10 each side
- **Cable Fly** — 3 × 12
- **Rear Delt Fly** — 3 × 15
- **Ab Wheel Rollout** — 3 × 8
- **Suitcase Carry** — 3 × 20 metres each side. Loaded carries are excellent for ski-specific core and hip stability.

---

### WEEKS 6–8 — PHASE 2 PROGRESSION

**Week 6:** Add 2.5–5 kg to all barbell movements where the Week 5 final set was completed with good form. Increase the step-up box height to 25 cm if the 15 cm version was pain-free. Add a **Nordic Hamstring Curl (eccentric only, assisted)** — 3 × 5 — to Day A. Have the client kneel on a mat with you holding his ankles, and he lowers himself as slowly as possible, catching himself with his hands. This is one of the most evidence-supported exercises for hamstring and posterior-chain resilience.

**Week 7:** Introduce a **Bulgarian Split Squat (rear foot elevated, front foot forward, 0–70° front knee flexion)** — 3 × 8 each side — on Day C, replacing the goblet squat. Use light dumbbells initially. This is a significant unilateral challenge and the closest ski-specific movement in the programme so far. Monitor the right knee closely. If there is any discomfort, revert to the goblet squat and revisit in Week 9.

**Week 8:** Deload. Same protocol as Week 4 — reduce volume by one set per exercise, reduce loads by 15%. Use this week to reassess the client's knee pain scores across the previous three weeks, review movement quality, and plan Phase 3 loading targets.

---

## PHASE 3 — WEEKS 9–12
### *Ski-Specific Strength and Resilience: Peak Loading and Transfer*

By now the client should have a strong posterior chain, meaningful unilateral leg strength, and a knee that tolerates 70–80° of loaded flexion without complaint. Phase 3 pushes toward 80–90° depth where appropriate, increases overall training load, and introduces ski-specific movement patterns — lateral loading, rotational stability, and sustained isometric holds that mimic the demands of carving turns. Four days per week, same split as Phase 2.

---

### WEEK 9

**Day A — Lower Body Power-Endurance**

Warm-up: 10 minutes stationary bike, full comfortable range. TKE band work, glute bridges, and now add **Wall Sit (30 seconds at 60° knee flexion)** as a ski-specific isometric primer.

- **Barbell Back Squat (to 80–85° depth, heels elevated)** — 4 × 6. This is the programme's first barbell squat. The heel elevation and controlled depth make it appropriate at this stage. If the client has not back-squatted before or is uncomfortable with the bar position, use a safety squat bar or continue with the goblet squat at increased load.
- **Barbell RDL** — 4 × 6, heavier than Phase 2 peak loads
- **Bulgarian Split Squat (dumbbells, progressing to barbell)** — 4 × 8 each side
- **Nordic Hamstring Curl (eccentric, less assistance than Week 6)** — 3 × 6
- **Hip Thrust (barbell, heavy)** — 4 × 8
- **Wall Sit (isometric, 60° knee angle)** — 3 × 45 seconds. This directly mimics the sustained quad demand of holding a ski tuck or absorbing a mogul field.

**Day B — Upper Body Strength**

- **Barbell Bench Press** — 4 × 5 (heavier than Phase 2)
- **Weighted Pull-Up** — 4 × 5
- **Pendlay Row** — 4 × 6
- **Dumbbell Shoulder Press** — 3 × 8
- **Cable Face Pull** — 3 × 15
- **Tricep Dip (bodyweight or assisted)** — 3 × 10
- **Hammer Curl** — 3 × 12

**Day C — Ski-Specific Lower Body**

- **Lateral Step-Up (stepping sideways onto a 25–30 cm box)** — 3 × 10 each side. The lateral plane is where skiing lives. This is the most ski-specific loaded movement in the programme.
- **Single-Leg Leg Press (both legs, compare loads)** — 4 × 8 each side. By now any strength asymmetry should be narrowing. If the right leg is still more than 15% weaker than the left, prioritise right-leg volume.
- **Seated Leg Curl** — 4 × 10
- **Lateral Band Walk (with mini band above knees, slight squat position)** — 3 × 20 steps each direction
- **Suitcase Carry** — 4 × 25 metres each side, heavier than Phase 2
- **Copenhagen Plank (full — top leg straight on bench)** — 3 × 25 seconds each side

**Day D — Upper Body and Rotational Core**

- **Overhead Press** — 4 × 5
- **Weighted Chin-Up** — 4 × 5
- **Cable Row (single arm, standing)** — 3 × 10 each side
- **Cable Woodchop (high to low, heavy)** — 4 × 10 each side. Rotational core strength is essential for absorbing and redirecting forces while skiing.
- **Landmine Rotation** — 3 × 10 each side. A controlled, loaded rotational exercise that trains the obliques and thoracic spine — both critical for ski turns.
- **Farmer's Carry** — 3 × 30 metres

---

### WEEKS 10–12 — PHASE 3 PROGRESSION

**Week 10:** Increase barbell squat and RDL loads by 5 kg. Extend wall sit holds to 60 seconds. Add a **Skater Squat (also called a single-leg squat to box, landing on a low surface behind)** — 3 × 6 each side — as a controlled, non-impact unilateral challenge. This is the most demanding knee exercise in the programme and should only be introduced if the client is completely pain-free on all Phase 3 exercises.

**Week 11:** Peak loading week. This is the hardest week of the programme. Push all compound lifts to the heaviest loads the client can handle with excellent form. Extend wall sits to 75 seconds. Add a second set of lateral step-ups. The client should feel genuinely challenged but not broken. Sleep and nutrition become especially important this week.

**Week 12:** Deload and reassessment. Reduce volume and load as in previous deload weeks. Use the sessions to perform a full movement reassessment — compare squat depth, single-leg strength symmetry, and pain scores against Week 1 baselines. Discuss return-to-skiing timeline with the surgeon and physiotherapist. If all markers are positive, the client is well-positioned to begin on-snow preparation.

---

## RECOVERY PROTOCOLS

**Between sessions:** Encourage 7–9 hours of sleep as the primary recovery tool. On rest days, 20–30 minutes of low-intensity activity — walking, easy cycling, or swimming — is preferable to complete inactivity, as it promotes blood flow to the healing tissue without loading it.

**Post-session knee management:** If the knee is warm or mildly swollen after a session, 10–15 minutes of ice wrapped in a cloth is appropriate. Elevation for 20 minutes post-session is also helpful in the early phases. If swelling is present before a session, do not progress load that day — maintain or regress.

**Mobility work:** Spend 5–10 minutes after every session on hip flexor stretching (the right hip flexor in particular tends to tighten after meniscal injuries as the body guards the knee), calf and Achilles stretching, and thoracic spine rotation. Thoracic mobility is underrated for skiing — a stiff upper back forces the lower back and knees to compensate on the slopes.

**Physiotherapy liaison:** If the client has an ongoing relationship with a physiotherapist, share this programme with them. They may wish to add specific meniscal loading progressions or manual therapy alongside the gym work. This programme is designed to complement, not replace, that relationship.

---

## NUTRITION GUIDANCE

Since you have not specified a detailed nutrition brief, the following are general principles appropriate for this client's goals.

**Protein:** Adequate protein intake is the single most important nutritional variable for both muscle building and connective tissue repair. A target of 1.8–2.2 grams of protein per kilogram of bodyweight per day is appropriate. Distribute this across three to four meals rather than concentrating it in one sitting, as muscle protein synthesis is optimised by regular leucine stimulation throughout the day.

**Collagen and Vitamin C:** There is emerging evidence that 15 grams of collagen peptides taken with 50 mg of vitamin C approximately 30–60 minutes before training may support cartilage and connective tissue synthesis. Given the meniscal context, this is a low-risk, potentially beneficial addition.

**Energy balance:** This client is not in a fat-loss phase — he is in a tissue-repair and strength-building phase. Eating at or slightly above maintenance calories will support both goals. Aggressive caloric restriction during this period would compromise recovery and slow the return to skiing.

**Carbohydrates:** Do not fear carbohydrates. Glycogen availability supports training quality, and training quality drives adaptation. A moderate-to-high carbohydrate intake around training sessions is appropriate.

**Hydration:** Synovial fluid — which lubricates the knee joint — is water-dependent. Adequate hydration (at minimum 35 ml per kg of bodyweight per day) is directly relevant to joint health, not just general performance.

---

## RETURN-TO-SKIING BENCHMARKS

Before the client steps back into ski boots, the following physical benchmarks should ideally be met:

1. **Strength symmetry:** Single-leg leg press strength on the right leg should be within 10% of the left leg.
2. **Pain-free range:** The client should be able to perform a bodyweight squat to 90° without pain or swelling.
3. **Wall sit endurance:** 60 seconds at 60° knee flexion without pain.
4. **Surgeon and physio sign-off:** Non-negotiable. This programme prepares the body; the medical team confirms readiness.
5. **Proprioception:** Single-leg balance on the right leg for 30 seconds with eyes closed, without excessive wobble. This can be tested informally at the end of each phase.

If all five benchmarks are met at the end of Week 12, the client has an excellent physical foundation for a return to recreational skiing. A ski-specific conditioning block — including balance board work, lateral agility, and progressive on-snow exposure — would be the logical next step, ideally guided by a ski coach alongside continued gym work.

---

*This programme was designed for a specific client profile and should be adjusted based on ongoing pain monitoring, surgeon guidance, and individual response to training. When in doubt, regress before you progress.*
